title: CMMI 2021 strategy: Driving Health System Transformation
questions: What was the CMS Innovation Center's 2021 strategy?
What are CMMI's five strategic objectives from the strategy refresh?
What did CMMI learn from its first decade of models?
What does 'Driving Health System Transformation' refer to?
summary: In 2021 the CMS Innovation Center published a strategy refresh titled "Driving Health System Transformation - A Strategy for the CMS Innovation Center's Second Decade." Its vision was a health system that achieves equitable outcomes through high-quality, affordable, person-centered care. The strategy was organized around five objectives: drive accountable care, advance health equity, support care innovations, improve access by addressing affordability, and partner to achieve system transformation. It was framed by lessons from the Center's first decade and more than 50 launched models, including that health equity should be embedded in every model, that the portfolio should be streamlined to reduce overlap, that transformation supports help providers take on risk, that model design had not always ensured broad provider participation, and that complex financial benchmarks had undermined effectiveness. The document reported that only six of those 50-plus models produced statistically significant Medicare savings and four met the statutory expansion bar. The headline target was placing all Medicare Parts A and B beneficiaries, and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries, in accountable care relationships by 2030. The 2025 strategy later replaced this framework; the 2021 document now sits in CMS's strategy archive.

summary: The 2021 strategy refresh set the Innovation Center's best-known target under its first objective, Drive Accountable Care: all Medicare beneficiaries with Parts A and B should be in a care relationship with accountability for quality and total cost of care by 2030, and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries should be too. CMS said it would set interim targets to track progress. Accountable entities could include physician groups, hospitals, Medicare Advantage plans, PACE programs and Medicaid managed care plans, depending on the program. The baseline the strategy cited was that in 2020, 67% of Medicare Part A and B enrollees were either in MA plans or attributed to an ACO through the Shared Savings Program or an Innovation Center model; within Traditional Medicare, its 2021 figure showed about 35% (10.7 million) in Shared Savings Program ACOs and about 7% (2.3 million) in other ACO-like models. CMS continued to report against the goal through January 2025 (53.4% of Traditional Medicare). The 2025 strategy keeps moving beneficiaries into accountable care as an objective but does not restate the 2030 date, and the February 2026 ACO fact sheet does not mention it.

summary: On May 13, 2025, the CMS Innovation Center posted a new strategy, "CMS Innovation Center Strategy to Make America Healthy Again." Its vision is healthier lives through evidence-based prevention, patient empowerment, and greater choice and competition, and those three ideas are the strategy's pillars. They sit on a foundational principle of protecting federal taxpayers in every model and activity. Objectives under that principle include making all model tests fiscally sound, requiring models to carry downside financial risk, and reducing the role of state government in rate setting. The strategy states no dated targets. It still aims to move Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries into accountable care arrangements, but without the 2030 deadline from the 2021 strategy, which now sits in an archive. The companion FAQ says the Center will update existing Original Medicare models, expand work in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid, and pursue multi-payer approaches with states. Models announced since then, including ACCESS, MAHA ELEVATE, BALANCE, WISeR, LEAD and the drug-pricing models, are the practical expression of this strategy. Trade press reported that CMMI Director Abe Sutton and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz presented the strategy on a webinar; the CMS page does not name them.

summary: On March 12, 2025, CMS announced Innovation Center portfolio changes aimed at aligning with the Center's statutory mandate to cut spending. Four models were to end early, by December 31, 2025: Maryland Total Cost of Care (originally through 2026, with Maryland moving into AHEAD), Primary Care First (through 2026), ESRD Treatment Choices (through 2027; mandatory, so ending it required rulemaking), and Making Care Primary (through 2034). CMS said the primary care changes did not signal a retreat from primary care. title: Section 1115A: CMMI's statutory authority
questions: What law created the CMS Innovation Center?
How much funding does CMMI get?

summary: The Innovation Center was created by the Affordable Care Act, which added section 1115A to the Social Security Act (codified at 42 U.S.C. 1315a). The section lets the Secretary test payment and service delivery models expected to reduce program spending while preserving or improving quality in Medicare, Medicaid and CHIP. Funding was $5 million for fiscal 2010 and $10 billion for fiscal 2011 through 2019, with another $10 billion for each later ten-year period, available until spent; at least $25 million a year must go to model testing. The Secretary may waive requirements of title XI, title XVIII and certain Medicaid provisions as needed to test models. The statute bars administrative or judicial review of model selection, participant and site selection, design, budget-neutrality determinations, termination or modification, and expansion decisions, and the Paperwork Reduction Act does not apply. The Secretary must report to Congress at least every other year beginning in 2012 on models tested, payments, expansions and evaluation results. CMS has described the law as requiring it to end or modify models expected to raise Medicare costs, the reason it gave for terminating the Medicare Advantage VBID model after 2025.

summary: Section 1115A(c) lets the Secretary expand a tested model in duration and scope, including nationwide, through rulemaking, if three conditions hold. The Secretary must find that expansion is expected to reduce spending without reducing quality or improve quality without increasing spending; the CMS Chief Actuary must certify that expansion would reduce, or not increase, net program spending; and the Secretary must find that expansion would not deny or limit coverage or benefits. CMS's Office of the Actuary lists certifications for the Pioneer ACO Model (savings certified April 10, 2015), the Diabetes Prevention Program (March 14, 2016, recertified November 1, 2017), Home Health Value-Based Purchasing, the repetitive scheduled non-emergent ambulance prior authorization model, and Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement. Those became, respectively, features absorbed into the Shared Savings Program, the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program expanded model, the nationwide Expanded HHVBP model (announced January 2021), a nationwide RSNAT program extended by MACRA, and the mandatory nationwide CJR-X model starting 2028. The 2021 strategy counted only four models meeting expansion requirements as of September 2021. BPCI Advanced, despite estimated net savings, was judged not to meet the criteria.

title: CBO 2023: CMMI increased federal spending in its first decade
questions: Did CMMI save money according to CBO?
What did CBO's 2023 report on the Innovation Center find?
How much did CMMI cost taxpayers from 2011 to 2020?
What does CBO project for CMMI in 2021-2030?
summary: In September 2023 the Congressional Budget Office reversed its original view of the Innovation Center. When the ACA passed in 2010, CBO projected CMMI would produce net savings; extended to 2011-2020, that original approach implied a $2.8 billion net reduction. Looking back, CBO estimated instead that CMMI's activities increased direct spending by $5.4 billion over 2011-2020, about 0.1% of net Medicare spending. The center spent $7.9 billion operating its models, while the models cut spending on health benefits by only $2.6 billion. Of 49 models with published evaluations in that decade, six produced statistically significant savings; four of those were certified for expansion. For 2021-2030 CBO projected another net increase of $1.3 billion, with $8.3 billion in operating costs offset by about $7.0 billion in benefit reductions, compared with $77.5 billion in net savings that its 2010 method would have implied. CBO said the estimates carry considerable uncertainty. The report is widely cited by both critics of CMMI and the 2025 strategy's emphasis on protecting taxpayers.

summary: CMS's own 2021 strategy refresh gave a candid scorecard of the Innovation Center's first ten years. Of more than 50 models launched, only six had generated statistically significant savings to Medicare as of September 2021: the Maryland All-Payer Model, the Repetitive Scheduled Non-Emergent Ambulance Transport (RSNAT) prior authorization model, the Home Health Value-Based Purchasing model, the ACO Investment Model, the Pioneer ACO Model, and the Medicare Care Choices Model. Four models had met the section 1115A(c) requirements for expansion in duration and scope: Pioneer ACO, the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program, RSNAT and HHVBP. CBO's 2023 review reached a similar count (six of 49 evaluated models with significant savings, four certified). Later results add to the picture, with BPCI Advanced reporting about $800 million in net savings over eight years and CJR certified for expansion, while models such as VBID, Oncology Care and Kidney Care Choices showed net costs in evaluations. CMS cited this record in both the 2021 strategy's call for fewer, simpler models and the 2025 strategy's focus on fiscal soundness.

title: Successor models and scaling pathways
questions: How do CMMI models scale besides formal expansion?
What is a successor model at CMMI?
Which CMMI models are successors of earlier models?
summary: In a January 13, 2025 blog post, Innovation Center leaders (Liz Fowler and colleagues) described ways a model can scale besides formal section 1115A(c) expansion. Model features can be written into other Medicare programs by rulemaking, as the ACO Investment Model's advance payments were added to the Shared Savings Program. Congress can adopt them, as it did with nationwide RSNAT prior authorization. Private payers can pick them up, as with the Accountable Health Communities social needs screening tool. And successor models can build on predecessors. The examples given: BPCI (2011-2018) led to BPCI Advanced and CJR (both 90-day episodes) and then the mandatory TEAM with 30-day post-discharge episodes; the Comprehensive ESRD Care Model (from 2015) led to ESRD Treatment Choices and Kidney Care Choices; and AHEAD serves as both a successor to Maryland's models and a multi-state scaling strategy. The post noted that AHEAD, Innovation in Behavioral Health and Transforming Maternal Health have eight- to ten-year performance periods. Later examples include LEAD succeeding ACO REACH and CJR-X expanding CJR.

summary: CMS reported on January 15, 2025 that 53.4% of people with Traditional Medicare, more than 14.8 million people, were in an accountable care relationship with a provider. That was 4.3 percentage points above January 2024 and, per CMS, the largest annual increase since it began tracking. CMS counts beneficiaries whose providers are in Shared Savings Program ACOs or Innovation Center accountable care models, plus other Innovation Center models focused on total cost of care, advanced primary care and specialty care. For 2025 the Shared Savings Program had 476 ACOs (228 approved applications: 55 new, 173 renewing or re-entering), more than 655,000 providers and about 11.2 million assigned beneficiaries, with 28 ACOs receiving advance investment payments. ACO REACH had 103 ACOs and about 2.5 million beneficiaries; Kidney Care Choices had 78 kidney contracting entities and 15 Kidney Care First practices serving about 240,000 people; and the new ACO Primary Care Flex Model began with 24 ACOs and about 349,000 beneficiaries. CMS framed the figures as progress toward the 2030 goal.

summary: CMS introduced its National Quality Strategy in a June 6, 2022 blog post by Michelle Schreiber, Adam Richards, Jean Moody-Williams and Lee Fleisher. The strategy aims for high-quality, safe care for all people across their care journey and across payers (Traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP, and Marketplace plans). It has eight goals: embed quality into the care journey; advance health equity; promote safety, with an aim of preventing all harm or death from health care errors; foster engagement; strengthen resiliency; embrace the digital age, including a full transition to digital quality measurement; incentivize innovation and technology adoption; and increase measure alignment. CMS's current quality strategy page describes the effort as evolving, now emphasizing prevention, wellness and chronic disease management, and lists its levers: quality data collection and exchange, engagement, reporting and feedback, standards and oversight, and coverage, payment and value-based models. The Universal Foundation measure set is the main vehicle for the alignment goal. It succeeded the 2012-2016 CMS Quality Strategy and the Meaningful Measures Initiative (2017).

summary: The Universal Foundation is CMS's core set of high-priority quality measures meant to be used across as many CMS quality and value-based programs as possible, to focus attention, reduce reporting burden, support digital measurement and allow comparison across programs. CMS leaders including Douglas Jacobs, Michelle Schreiber, Meena Seshamani, Daniel Tsai, Elizabeth Fowler and Lee Fleisher introduced it in a New England Journal of Medicine Perspective, "Aligning Quality Measures across CMS - The Universal Foundation," in early 2023. CMS's page lists 9 adult measures: colorectal and breast cancer screening, adult immunization status, controlling high blood pressure, hemoglobin A1c poor control, depression screening and follow-up, initiation and engagement of substance use disorder treatment, all-cause readmissions, and CAHPS overall ratings. The pediatric set has 13 measures, including well-child visits, immunizations, weight assessment, oral evaluation, asthma medication ratio, several behavioral health follow-up measures and CAHPS. summary: ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) is a voluntary Innovation Center ACO model for Traditional Medicare that began January 1, 2023 as the redesign of Global and Professional Direct Contracting, announced February 24, 2022. It runs four performance years through 2026 and is not accepting new applicants; LEAD replaces it in 2027. ACO types are Standard, New Entrant and High Needs Population. Under the Professional option the ACO shares 50% of savings and losses and receives Primary Care Capitation; under Global it bears 100% of savings and losses and can take Primary Care or Total Care Capitation, a monthly risk-adjusted payment covering all services. Beneficiaries keep free choice of providers. CMS's PY2024 reconciliation (released July 9, 2026) covered 115 ACOs and about 2.5 million beneficiaries: about $2.51 billion in gross savings (6.7% of adjusted benchmarks), $988.3 million net savings to CMS (2.6%) and $1.522 billion to ACOs (4.2%), up from $694.6 million to CMS in PY2023. CMS said 95% of its PY2024 net savings came from the 3% discount on Global benchmarks, and 96 of 115 ACOs earned net savings. CMS cautions that the formal evaluation, which uses a comparison group, measures impact differently. Participation fell to 74 ACOs and about 1.7 million beneficiaries in 2026.

summary: The Medicare Shared Savings Program is Medicare's permanent ACO program, created by the Affordable Care Act and run by CMS outside the Innovation Center's time-limited model authority. ACOs of physicians, hospitals, FQHCs, RHCs and other providers are held accountable for the quality and total cost of care of assigned Traditional Medicare beneficiaries and can share savings against a benchmark, with one-sided BASIC levels and two-sided BASIC and ENHANCED tracks. summary: The Pioneer ACO Model was an early Innovation Center ACO test for organizations already experienced in coordinated care. It ran January 1, 2012 through December 31, 2016, starting with 32 ACOs and ending with 9. In the first two years ACOs used shared savings and losses with higher potential reward and risk than the Shared Savings Program, settled only when spending fell outside a corridor set by minimum savings and loss rates. From year three, ACOs reaching a savings threshold could move much of their payment to a population-based payment. Pioneer was the first Innovation Center model certified by the CMS Office of the Actuary for expansion (certification of Pioneer savings dated April 10, 2015). The 2021 strategy lists it among six models with statistically significant savings and four meeting expansion requirements. Its design lessons, especially higher-risk tracks, informed later MSSP tracks and Next Generation ACO. The CMS directory classifies it as Authorized for Expansion even though the model itself ended in 2016.

summary: The Global and Professional Direct Contracting Model was the predecessor to ACO REACH. Its implementation period began October 1, 2020, the first performance period began April 1, 2021, and it ended December 31, 2022. summary: TEAM is a mandatory Innovation Center episode-based payment model for acute care hospitals paid under the IPPS in selected Core-Based Statistical Areas, listed in the FY 2025 IPPS final rule. Episodes cover lower extremity joint replacement, surgical hip and femur fracture treatment, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass graft and major bowel procedures, beginning with the inpatient stay or outpatient procedure and ending 30 days after discharge. Hospitals keep billing fee-for-service and are reconciled against a risk-adjusted target price covering Part A and B spending, earning or repaying the difference subject to a quality adjustment. Track 1 has no downside in year one (up to three years for safety-net hospitals); Track 2 offers lower risk and reward for safety-net, rural and similar hospitals in years 2-5; Track 3 carries higher risk and reward throughout. Hospitals must refer patients to primary care. The FY 2027 IPPS final rule (July 31, 2026) updated TEAM policies.

title: Innovation in Behavioral Health (IBH) Model
questions: What is the Innovation in Behavioral Health model?
Which states are in IBH?
How does IBH pay behavioral health practices?
summary: The Innovation in Behavioral Health Model is a state-based Innovation Center model that makes specialty behavioral health practices the hub for whole-person care for people with moderate to severe mental illness, substance use disorders or both, across Medicaid, Medicare and dual-eligible beneficiaries. It runs 2025-2032: a pre-implementation period from 2025 to 2027 and implementation from 2028 to 2032. CMS issued cooperative agreement awards on January 1, 2025 to three state Medicaid agencies, Michigan, New York and South Carolina, working with state mental health or substance use authorities, and plans up to eight states over the model's life. Practices receive infrastructure and capacity funding before implementation, then per-person-per-month payments with performance-based payments in 2028-2032. Practices serving Medicare and dual-eligible patients apply through a separate request for applications.

title: Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model
questions: What was the Accountable Health Communities model?
What is the AHC health-related social needs screening tool?
Did the Accountable Health Communities model reduce ED visits?
summary: The Accountable Health Communities Model tested whether systematically screening Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries for health-related social needs and connecting them to community services would improve outcomes and reduce costs. The performance period ran May 1, 2017 to April 30, 2022, with an optional extension to April 30, 2023. CMS selected 32 bridge organizations as local hubs (28 remained in April 2022). The Assistance Track randomized eligible high-risk beneficiaries to community service navigation or referral alone; the Alignment Track worked on aligning clinical and community services. Funding covered bridge organization infrastructure and staff, not the services themselves. CMS's summary of the final evaluation said the model reduced inpatient stays and ED visits, with variation by track and payer. Its lasting product is the AHC Health-Related Social Needs Screening Tool, which CMS says is in wide private-sector use.

title: Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program (MDPP) Expanded Model
questions: What is the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program?
Can MDPP be delivered online?
How are MDPP suppliers paid?
summary: The Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program is an expansion of the Diabetes Prevention Program model test run 2012-2015 with the YMCA under section 1115A(b). The CMS Chief Actuary certified the expansion on March 14, 2016 (recertified November 1, 2017), the first Innovation Center prevention model to qualify. CMS expanded it nationally through the CY 2017 and CY 2018 Physician Fee Schedule rules, and suppliers could bill from April 1, 2018. It is a Part B preventive service: a one-year CDC-recognized lifestyle program with 16 weekly core sessions and 6 monthly maintenance sessions, up to 22 sessions, for beneficiaries at risk of type 2 diabetes. CMS pays suppliers fee-for-service for attendance plus performance payments tied to weight loss. Sessions can be in person, live virtual or asynchronous online; the CY 2026 PFS final rule extended those flexibilities through December 31, 2029. The page lists 941 participating suppliers.

title: Medicare Advantage Value-Based Insurance Design (VBID) Model
questions: What was the MA VBID model?
Why did CMS end the VBID model?
How much did VBID cost Medicare?
What was the VBID hospice benefit component?
summary: The Medicare Advantage Value-Based Insurance Design Model let participating MA organizations tailor supplemental benefits and cost-sharing for enrollees with chronic conditions, low-income subsidy or dual eligibility, or residence in high-deprivation areas, offer Part D cost-sharing reductions, and run rewards and incentives programs. From CY2021 to CY2024 a hospice benefit component tested carving hospice into MA; CMS ended it December 31, 2024. The model's performance period began January 1, 2017. In CY2025, 62 MA organizations participated, projecting extra benefits for over seven million enrollees. On December 16, 2024 CMS announced VBID would terminate after CY2025 because of substantial, unmitigable costs: about $2.3 billion in CY2021 and $2.2 billion in CY2022 per evaluation findings, driven by faster risk score growth than in comparable plans, higher rebates and higher Part D spending. CMS said no viable policy changes could fix the costs and that the law required ending it. The model ended December 31, 2025 and should not be presented as an available option.

title: Part D Senior Savings Model
questions: What was the Part D Senior Savings Model?
How did the $35 insulin model work?
Why did the Part D Senior Savings Model end?
summary: The Part D Senior Savings Model was a voluntary Innovation Center model that ran January 1, 2021 to December 31, 2023. Participating Part D plans offered a broad set of insulins at a stable, maximum $35 monthly copay, with manufacturers (Eli Lilly, MannKind, Mylan/Viatris, Novo Nordisk and Sanofi in 2022-2023) supplying discounts. In CY2022, 2,159 plans from 106 sponsors participated, covering more than 17 million enrollees; in CY2023, more than 2,500 MA-PD and standalone drug plans. The Inflation Reduction Act then capped Part D insulin cost-sharing at $35 per month's supply for each covered insulin from January 1, 2023, with no deductible, making the benefit universal in Part D. The model concluded at the end of 2023, and CMS has posted a final evaluation. It is a clear case of an Innovation Center test feeding into legislation.

title: Expanded Home Health Value-Based Purchasing Model
questions: What is the Expanded HHVBP model?
How much can home health payments change under HHVBP?
Was the original HHVBP model successful?
summary: The original Home Health Value-Based Purchasing Model began January 1, 2016 in nine states and was finalized in the CY 2016 home health PPS rule under section 1115A. CMS reports it produced an average 4.6% improvement in total performance scores and about $141 million in average annual Medicare savings. After certification, CMS announced on January 8, 2021 that it would expand the model nationwide. The Expanded HHVBP model covers all Medicare-certified home health agencies in the 50 states, DC and the territories: 2022 was a pre-implementation year, CY2023 the first performance year, and CY2025 the first payment year. Agencies are compared within larger- and smaller-volume cohorts, and Medicare fee-for-service payments are adjusted from -5% to +5% based on quality performance relative to peers. It is one of the few Innovation Center models to reach permanent national scale.

title: WISeR (Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction) Model
questions: What is the WISeR model?
Is CMS adding prior authorization to Original Medicare?
Which states are in WISeR?
Which vendors run WISeR?
summary: WISeR is an Innovation Center model that adds technology-assisted medical necessity review to Original Medicare for selected services in six states: New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona and Washington. It runs six performance years, January 1, 2026 through December 31, 2031. Targeted services include skin and tissue substitutes, electrical nerve stimulator implants and knee arthroscopy for osteoarthritis; inpatient-only, emergency and delay-sensitive services are excluded. Providers can request prior authorization from the vendor or their MAC, or accept post-service, pre-payment review. Participating technology companies, one per state (Cohere Health, Genzeon, Humata Health, Innovaccer, Virtix Health and Zyter), use AI and machine learning, with licensed clinicians making any non-payment recommendations. Vendors are paid a share of averted wasteful spending, adjusted for performance measures including provider experience. CMS states the model does not change coverage or payment policy, and MA enrollees are unaffected.

title: Cell and Gene Therapy (CGT) Access Model
questions: What is the Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model?
How many states joined the CGT Access Model?
Which sickle cell gene therapies are in the CGT model?
summary: The Cell and Gene Therapy Access Model is a voluntary multi-year Innovation Center model that initially targets access to gene therapies for people with sickle cell disease in Medicaid. CMS negotiates core terms with manufacturers, including price discounts and outcomes-based rebates tied to how patients fare, and each state decides whether to sign on; manufacturers then pay supplemental rebates to participating states. The participating manufacturers are Genetix Biotherapeutics and Vertex Pharmaceuticals. States joined between January 2025 and January 2026, and there are 34 state participants (32 states, DC and Puerto Rico), eight of which received cooperative agreement funding. Outcomes-based agreements of this kind need long patient follow-up.

title: Medicare $2 Drug List Model (not pursued)

Is the $2 drug list happening?
Why was the $2 Drug List model canceled?

It was never implemented. In its March 12, 2025 portfolio announcement CMS said it would not pursue the $2 Drug List or the Accelerating Clinical Evidence model, citing the January 20, 2025 rescission of Executive Order 14087. The CMS model directory lists it as Not Active. This entry should be used to answer questions about the model's fate, not as an available program.

title: GLOBE (Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing) Model
questions: What is the GLOBE model?
Is CMS using international reference pricing for Part B drugs?
When does GLOBE start?
summary: GLOBE is a mandatory Innovation Center model that charges drug manufacturers rebates on certain Original Medicare Part B drugs whose prices exceed those paid in economically comparable countries, using an international benchmark in an alternative rebate calculation. It covers single-source drugs and sole-source biologics in oncology, rheumatology, immunology, ophthalmology and endocrinology classes (with exceptions) where annual Original Medicare spending exceeds $100 million, with benchmarks drawn from 19 reference countries such as Canada, Japan and the United Kingdom. The proposed rule was published December 23, 2025 and CMS has released the final rule. The model launches January 1, 2027 and runs through March 31, 2032, with reduced beneficiary coinsurance from April 1, 2027, and rebate reconciliation into 2034. The directory lists it as Active even though the performance period has not begun.

title: GUARD (Guarding U.S. Medicare Against Rising Drug Costs) Model

Is there an international pricing model for Part D drugs?
Is GUARD final?
summary: GUARD is a proposed mandatory Innovation Center model that would have manufacturers pay rebates on certain Part D drugs whose prices exceed a benchmark based on prices in comparable countries, effectively modifying the Part D inflation rebate to use an international rather than domestic benchmark. It would apply to sole-source drugs and biologics in listed therapeutic classes, such as antineoplastics, cardiovascular agents and antivirals, in randomly selected geographic areas covering about 25% of Part D enrollees. Participants would be manufacturers, not providers. CMS issued a notice of proposed rulemaking with comments due February 23, 2026; the proposed period is January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2031, with reconciliation into 2033. As of this entry the model page showed it as proposed and not finalized.

Manufacturers must have an active Medicaid Drug Rebate Program agreement; AstraZeneca, Pfizer and EMD Serono have announced agreements. CMS says the model launched in January 2026 for five years, that all states and Puerto Rico have applied, and that state Medicaid agencies have until September 30, 2026 to finalize applications. title: BALANCE Model and Medicare GLP-1 Bridge

Will Medicare cover GLP-1s for weight loss?
What is the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge?
summary: BALANCE (Better Approaches to Lifestyle and Nutrition for Comprehensive hEalth) is a voluntary Innovation Center model to widen access to GLP-1 drugs and lifestyle support for people with obesity or overweight in Medicaid and Medicare. CMS negotiates lower prices directly with manufacturers; eligible drugs must be FDA-approved, or expected to be by January 1, 2027, for weight management and show average weight loss of at least 9.5% in a randomized trial. State Medicaid agencies can join from May 2026 through January 1, 2027, and Medicaid patients get a manufacturer-provided lifestyle program at no cost; coverage depends on state and manufacturer participation and may require prior authorization. Part D sponsors may participate later, but BALANCE is not expected to launch in Medicare in 2027. A separate short-term Medicare GLP-1 Bridge demonstration gives eligible Part D enrollees access to certain GLP-1s from July 1, 2026 through December 31, 2027.

title: ACCESS (Advancing Chronic Care with Effective, Scalable Solutions) Model
questions: What is the ACCESS model?
How does ACCESS pay for technology-enabled chronic care?
Which conditions are in ACCESS?
summary: ACCESS is a voluntary 10-year Innovation Center model testing a new Original Medicare payment for technology-supported chronic care. It began July 5, 2026 with rolling participant starts, and new tracks start April 1, 2027. Initial tracks: early cardio-kidney-metabolic (hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity with central adiposity, prediabetes), cardio-kidney-metabolic (diabetes, CKD 3a-3b, atherosclerotic heart disease), musculoskeletal pain, and behavioral health (depression and anxiety); heart failure, COPD, substance use disorder and tobacco cessation are planned for 2027. Participants receive recurring Outcome-Aligned Payments to manage a patient's condition, with full payment depending on the share of patients reaching measurable health targets above a rising annual threshold. Rural patients carry a fixed adjustment, and primary care and referring clinicians can bill a co-management payment. Participants must be Part B-enrolled organizations with a physician clinical director; CMS reports 160-plus participants.

title: MAHA ELEVATE Model

summary: MAHA ELEVATE (Make America Healthy Again: Enhancing Lifestyle and Evaluating Value-based Approaches Through Evidence) is a voluntary Innovation Center model that will fund up to 30 cooperative agreements, about $100 million over a three-year performance period, for organizations delivering evidence-based whole-person lifestyle and functional medicine services to Original Medicare beneficiaries alongside conventional care. Proposals must include nutrition or physical activity, and three awards are reserved for dementia interventions. Cohort 1 applications closed May 15, 2026, awards are expected in fall 2026, cohort 1 launches in October 2026, and a second cohort follows in 2027. It is the most direct expression of the 2025 strategy's prevention pillar. As a funding opportunity, it has no effectiveness results yet.

title: Ambulatory Specialty Model (ASM)
questions: What is the Ambulatory Specialty Model?
Which specialists must participate in ASM?
How large are ASM payment adjustments?
summary: The Ambulatory Specialty Model is a mandatory Innovation Center model with five performance years, January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2031, holding specialists accountable for care of two costly conditions. The heart failure cohort covers cardiologists; the low back pain cohort covers anesthesiology, pain management, interventional pain management, neurosurgery, orthopedic surgery and physical medicine and rehabilitation. Specialists are included if they are attributed at least 20 relevant episodes a year and practice in a selected area, roughly a quarter of CBSAs and metropolitan divisions. Performance on quality, episode-based cost, improvement activities and interoperability, built on MIPS Value Pathways, determines an ASM-specific adjustment to later Part B professional claims, from -9% to +9% in the first two years rising to -12% to +12% by the final year. CMS has posted the final 2027 participant list; the directory lists the model as Announced.

title: Rural Community Hospital Demonstration
questions: What is the Rural Community Hospital Demonstration?
How are hospitals paid in the RCH demonstration?
How long does the RCH demonstration run?
summary: The Rural Community Hospital Demonstration is a statutory demonstration created by section 410A of the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003, not an Innovation Center 1115A model, that pays small rural hospitals too large to be critical access hospitals on a cost basis for inpatient services. It began in 2004 in the 10 least populated states with up to 15 hospitals; the ACA expanded it to 20 states and 30 hospitals; the 21st Century Cures Act opened it to all states with priority for the 20 least densely populated; and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 extended it through June 30, 2028. Participants get reasonable cost in the base year, then the lesser of actual cost or an inflation- and case-mix-adjusted target. The law requires budget neutrality, which CMS achieves by reducing national inpatient rates. Ten more hospitals were selected to start in 2025, with agreements through June 30, 2028.

title: Frontier Community Health Integration Project (FCHIP) Demonstration

Eligible CAHs are in Alaska, Montana, Nevada, North Dakota and Wyoming, states where at least 65% of counties have six or fewer residents per square mile; five CAHs participate. The initial demonstration ran August 1, 2016 to July 31, 2019, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 authorized an extension starting with cost report periods beginning on or after January 1, 2022.

summary: The Medicare Care Choices Model let eligible beneficiaries receive supportive hospice-type services from participating hospices while continuing other Medicare-covered care, including treatment for their terminal condition, which standard hospice rules otherwise require them to give up. Cohort 1 began January 1, 2016 and cohort 2 January 1, 2018; both ended December 31, 2021. CMS expected about 30 hospices, later expanded eligibility to more than 140, and 82 were participating as of June 2020. Hospices received $200 to $400 per beneficiary per month for model services. CMS's 2021 strategy lists MCCM among the six Innovation Center models with statistically significant Medicare savings in the first decade.

title: Initiative to Reduce Avoidable Hospitalizations Among Nursing Facility Residents

summary: This Innovation Center initiative targeted avoidable hospitalizations of long-stay nursing facility residents. Phase One (September 2012 to September 2016) funded seven enhanced care and coordination provider organizations (ECCPs) to place clinical staff and supports in facilities.
